newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: U.S. envoy shuttles to Cape in bid to save Kinshasa.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy shuttles to Cape in bid to save Kinshasa.

text.p: U.S. envoy Bill Richardson kept up his fast-paced diplomatic shuttle across southern Africa on Tuesday, flying to Cape Town from Botswana for further urgent talks to avert a battle for the Zairean capital, Kinshasa.

The rebel army of Laurent Kabila was reported to be within one or two days march of the city of five million. It was not clear what specific measures Richardson was discussing that would prevent a battle for the city.

U.S. official sources in Cape Town said Richardson was heading directly for talks with South Africa's deputy president Thabo Mbeki, who is also playing a role in securing a peaceful end to the crumbling, 32-year-old rule of Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko.

In the past week, President Clinton's envoy has held talks with Mobutu, Kabila and the leaders of most of Zaire's nine African neighbours, which would be threatened by the collapse of the vast central African state.

Earlier on Tuesday in the northern Botswana border town of Kasane, Richardson met Ugandan leader Yoweri Museveni, Zimbabwe's President Robert Mugabe and Tanzania's Benjamin Mkapa for more than an hour.
"I have received helpful advice from the three presidents on how to procure a peaceful transition of power in Zaire," he told reporters afterwards.
"I believe that the peace talks initiated by President (Nelson) Mandela of South Africa will eventually lead to a peaceful transition," he added.

Richardson, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations and President Bill Clinton's envoy in the Zaire crisis, reiterated that he was seeking a "soft landing" to prevent possible bloodshed and chaos in Kinshasa.
Mobutu's spokesman said the president would travel to Gabon on Wednesday to attend a meeting of heads of state and would return to the capital Kinshasa on Friday.
Richardson told reporters in Botswana he hoped the evacuation of Americans and other foreign nationals from Kinshasa could still be avoided, but added that contingency plans would remain in place.
